Considerations were given to initial conditions, whether the systems were bound or not, and the influence of randomness associated with orbital eccentricity. Key aspects explored included the distribution of final orbital eccentricities and the relationship between these eccentricities and initial conditions. Additionally, our investigation looked at how initial orbital configurations and mass ratios affected system behavior, including three-body scattering events. We also analyzed how these factors influenced three-body exchange and escape probabilities. Ultimately, our study offered updated, more accurate estimates of escape probabilities, particularly for cases where orbital eccentricity was significant.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors for J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically for central 0-10% and semi-peripheral 20-40% events. The factors were determined both individually for each meson and in ratio form, and were compared with LHC experiments from past years and theoretical models, considering magnetic fields and quark interactions. The findings were further analyzed in terms of charmed quark distributions, and this comparison was used to constrain model parameters and understand the behavior of these mesons under various conditions.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When modifying a software product, it is crucial to ensure that changes do
not alter the product's behavior, otherwise it may lead to test cases that were
previously passed, now failing. Since tracing back individual product components
that impact test execution can be time-consuming, a regression analysis tool is
essential to identify the cause of test failures, optimizing development time.
Using a data-driven method, such as machine learning, can effectively address this
problem. However, the effectiveness of machine learning methods relies on the
quality of the data provided. In this context, a new sensor, the test execution
log, offers valuable insights into test suite运行. As a result, a new regression
predictor called ReRerun, based on the TeRrE system, uses data from test execution
logs to predict the tests that are likely to fail upon re-running, allowing for
the identification of changes in software products more efficiently. To validate
Rererun\'s effectiveness, we evaluated its performance against four well-known
baselines, which also analyzed test execution logs. The results from a real-world
industrial project revealed that ReRerun outperformed the baseline methods by a
considerable margin, with an accuracy of 67.4% vs. 47.9%, demonstrating the
predictor\'s reliability and dependability in identifying tests that are likely to
fail upon re-running.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation by leveraging established methods and incorporating real-time data from patient interaction records. Specifically, we apply a Transformer-based method to analyze data, including Ecological Momentary Assessment and Electronic Health Records, from mentally ill patients. Our results show that using only Ecological Momentary Assessment data, the proposed technique achieves an area under the curve of 0.61 in an early-stage setting and 0.64 in a late-stage setting. Furthermore, combining Ecological Momentary Assessment and Electronic Health Records data improves the area under the curve to 0.67 in the early-stage setting and yields nearly identical results in the late-stage setting, indicating minimal additional gain. Notably, the proposed technique enables precise short-term and individualized predictions of suicidal ideation, which are more accurate than those obtained from Electronic Health Records data alone.

Our research involves measuring linear polarization in X-rays using the Chandra Satellite's Polarimetric Imaging Calibrator, focusing on the synchrotron emission of SNR Cassiopeia A. RICI's polarization detection capabilities have been thoroughly tested and validated against simulated and actual unpolarized and linearly polarized sources. Our study found a polarization mean of 19.5% with standard deviation of 3.7% for the Chandra's synchrotron emission of CAS A. However, this figure is likely an overestimation of the true polarization mean, as a significant portion of the standard deviation stems from systematics associated with SNR Cassiopeia A's non-uniform thermal emission. Our research confirms a line of sight magnetic field alignment between the synchrotron and thermal components, demonstrating magnetic field uniformity across the intermixed medium of thermal energy in CAS A. Our analysis also revealed varying polarization standards, ranging from a mean of 26.4% with a standard deviation of 2.1% in cooler regions to a mean of 23.1% with a standard deviation of 3.3% in hotter regions of SNR Cassiopeia A. Our research confirms a line of sight magnetic field alignment between the synchrotron and thermal components, demonstrating uniform magnetic fields operating throughout the SNR Cassiopeia A's intermixed medium. Our findings have been published in The Astrophysical Journal on April 1,

Consider a set of n distinct numbers, and let B be the minimum maximum value of a subset with a given length. Erdos proposed a conjecture suggesting B's upper limit follows a specific pattern related to logarithmic and linear components. This conjecture was later refined by Fuge and Gyarmati with alternative notions. In the context of the original conjecture, we verify it for n up to 41, and for n greater than or equal to 42 with a modified step size. Further analysis shows a related maximum value, C, complies with a specific formula involving a specific sequence and a linear pattern. This involves verifying the accuracy of the OEIS sequence up to a specific number of elements, and also deriving a specific inequality involving a specific sequence and a specific number.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density are explored using two distinct theoretical concepts: dense nuclear matter and dense deconfined matter. It's anticipated that the sound velocity of dense nuclear matter increases with density, ultimately approaching a maximum velocity of light. The equation of state of dense nuclear matter which produces such a sound velocity trend is connected to its density through its polytropic index. The creation of smaller and smaller neutron stars is linked to an increase in the sound velocity of dense matter. Additionally, an increase in the maximum mass of neutron stars also indicates the presence of a peak in the sound velocity curve. The influence of a high sound velocity in dense nuclear matter results in a maximum mass greater than three times the mass of the sun. If the sound velocity in dense nuclear matter is not restricted, other variables such as the maximum mass of neutron stars and the radius of 1.4-solar-mass neutron stars can be precisely determined. The inclusion of a high sound velocity in dense nuclear matter produces a distinct pattern of a sound velocity trough located between the density ranges of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density. The trough corresponds to a deconfined matter phase and is accompanied by a minimum in the phase transition density. Should a first order phase transition from nuclear matter to deconfined matter occur, binary neutron star mergers may produce a remnant neutron star or black hole. If the remnant is a neutron star, it will

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as the compass state, which also exhibits equivalent statistical properties. Both proposed and compass states display analogous phase space structures. These new composite states display greater stability in terms of shot-to-shot variations when compared to the compass state, making them more suitable for applications in quantum metrology, while still achieving Heisenberg limited sensitivity.

During gas-liquid interfaces that are irregular in the direction parallel to gravity, the local curvature can significantly affect fluid dynamics. To effectively capture this behavior, we employ skeletonization, reducing the interface's complex geometry to a more manageable representation consisting of critical curves and surfaces where the curvature vanishes. Although this approach is computationally demanding, recent research suggests that even a basic approximation of the interface, limited to these critical points, can accurately predict the dynamics of the system.

In our work, we introduce an efficient algorithm for identifying these critical points, even when the interface extends infinitely in the directions parallel to gravity. This is achieved by identifying the maximal inversion-symmetric approximation of the interface, then extracting the critical points from the boundary of this approximation. Such an approximation, known as 'Peierls-Nelson' in statistical physics, finds applications beyond fluid dynamics, making our findings particularly relevant to the study of the system's behavior.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with glycan compounds, and this behavior is likely present in nature. This discovery has significant implications, as it sheds light on how these viruses navigate and interact with their environment. To understand the mechanisms behind the viruses' movement, researchers developed a mathematical model that incorporates the influence of the viruses' spike proteins and their response to the surrounding glycan landscape. The results of the study indicate that the viruses exhibit a unique behavior, getting stuck in localized areas and remaining there for extended periods, which may offer an evolutionary advantage by increasing their chances of infecting host cells.

We examined over 3000 edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS database, categorizing them by the presence of a bar, spiral arms, or ring structure, and distinguishing between 'U'- and 'S'-shaped configurations. A total of 169 U-ringed and 354 U-spiral, 2864 S-ringed and 23,733 S-spiral galaxies were identified. Our analysis revealed significant differences between u- and s- and r- and s- groups in terms of number, color, and star formation rates.

U-type warped disks are predominantly bluer than both S-type warped disks and U-type ringed galaxies, indicating that they tend to have younger stellar populations. U-type ringed galaxies exhibit significant star formation, whereas warped disks of similar structure exhibit lower specific star formation rates, up to two orders of magnitude lower.

It was also observed that U-type galaxies, regardless of ring or spiral configuration, are more likely to exhibit irregular, loosely wound arms or edges, in contrast to S-type galaxies with smoother, more tightly wound features. This difference is particularly noticeable when comparing U- and r- shaped galaxies without bars, suggesting a distinct evolutionary path for these distinct morphological types.

Our findings suggest that the primary difference between outer- and inner- shaped features in these distinct morphological types may be influenced by distinct formation processes, suggesting that the evolution of disk galaxies is complex and influenced

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Compounds composed of perovskites exhibit unique properties due to their arrangement of atoms in a cubic structure, with varying elements influencing phonon behavior. We investigate how atomic circulation within these cubic crystals gives rise to chiral phonons, demonstrating that such phonons can be manipulated by adjusting the crystal's symmetry and stoichiometry. By analyzing phonon dispersion, our research indicates that heavier atoms tend to form dominant local modes in certain directions when the crystal symmetry is distorted. To validate this phenomenon, we focus on a perovskite compound doped with strontium, employing mean-field theory to demonstrate that introducing shearing motion results in the emergence of chiral phonons, influenced by atomic masses and positions, particularly in Sr$_2$IrO$_4$.

In insulators, Born effective charges relate to how the position of individual electrons influences the overall movement of whole atoms.
We have created a new set of checks to ensure the accuracy of machine learning potentials, specifically targeting the validity of Born effective charges and dynamical matrices at a material's Gamma point.
Our method involves using a precise measure of error called the non-adiabatic correction, which helps us evaluate the reliability of machine learning potentials.
By applying this framework to various types of errors and using a test case of a machine learning potential for MgO, we found that the non-adiabatic correction follows specific mathematical relationships with temperature- related fluctuations and is primarily driven by a particular type of electronic response.
Additionally, we developed and utilized an analytical correction technique called the time-dependent perturbation correction that can adapt to different scenarios.
We demonstrated that this correction is essential for obtaining accurate results about phonon behavior in MgO.

We are investigating the role of thermal fluctuations in incompressible turbulence.
Our analysis indicates that thermal forces become significant at length scales close to or smaller than a newly defined Kolmogorov length, defined as (ν κ/B^2)^(3/4), where ν represents kinematic viscosity, κ is the mean curvature rate, and B^2 is the specific kinetic energy density. This newly defined length scale carries dimensions of length and varies based on specific turbulence conditions. Utilizing a reduced simulation model, we found that thermal forces can cause a transition from turbulent behavior to a laminar state when the P\'{e}cl\'{e}t number, a parameter representing the ratio of viscous forces to heat conduction, is surpassed. This suggests a potential mechanism for the complete laminarization of turbulent flows, analogous to laminarization through heat conduction, although we note that a more comprehensive theoretical framework for this phenomenon remains to be developed.

Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric response, which consists of a polarisation proportional to electric field and a magnetic field response, both influenced by a topological invariant under time-reversal symmetry. In the absence of this symmetry however, the same invariant collapses resulting in a $\theta$-term in the effective action, thereby modifying the electromagnetic response. The researchers in this study propose a method to define this term within their 3D topological insulator model, which involves an understanding of the three-dimensional Berry phase. Surprisingly, this approach yields an ambiguous result with two potential solutions differing by quantised amounts. In this context, the researchers also introduce an alternative method using a cut integration, eliminating reliance on time-reversal symmetry and also producing the same quantised ambiguity. In order to resolve this ambiguity however, the researchers introduce a regularisation scheme that preserves gauge invariance, which in turn results in one of the two solutions and thereby provides an independent characterization for 3D topological insulators.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, especially when the modulation's map exhibits mode locking, characteristic of laminar chaos. For the first time, this find is demonstrated through numerical analysis of the delayed logistic equation. For certain parameter settings, this chaos-periodic switching can be replaced by border collision chaos, resulting in an even more pronounced increase in the diffusion coefficient. Moreover, a brief analysis indicates that this increase in diffusion is not merely an isolated occurrence but an underlying general phenomenon applicable to a wider range of systems with delayed nonlinearity.

We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018).

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are vital to software creation and can be used to link past discussions to the code they refer to. Consequently, it becomes possible to predict which individuals or groups should be consulted in the face of future challenges. An emerging field known as design mining, a sub-area of code commenting mining, seeks to extract implicit design knowledge from version control systems and other sources related to software development. This knowledge can then be made accessible to developers through static analysis and natural language processing. Current design mining studies concentrate on identifying patterns and providing a taxonomy, which can serve as a foundation for more complex applications. Our work seeks to expand upon this knowledge by exploring the extraction of domain-specific design patterns and taxonomy from design texts, which can then be leveraged for a range of downstream tasks. This research also seeks to identify the traits of effective design patterns, which can contribute to understanding design evolution and its applications.

A proposed model for dark energy and dark matter based on the idea that gravity emerges due to a homogeneous, isotropic momentum density with an exponentially decaying magnitude as it moves away from the origin. By considering the momentum's anisotropic velocity fields in the radial and tangential directions, the model generates pressure and can be used to study the behavior of the universe, including its acceleration, the interaction between dark energy and dark matter, and the evolution of the universe from the Past to a matter-dominated universe.

Proximal methods are a popular choice for optimizing nonsmooth functions due to their versatility in handling a broad class of problems. However, the standard iterative approach can become unfeasibly slow when the objective function is highly ill-conditioned. As a result, adapting this scheme to converge faster for such problems is highly desirable. We propose adding an acceleration factor into the standard iterative framework, making it applicable to both deterministic and stochastic settings. When paired with convex functions, our modified scheme is stochastic asymptotically unbiased. We support our theory with empirical evidence, showing the scheme/accelerated scheme outcomes.

We are investigating the properties of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with an arbitrary multiplicative identity. Several types of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals are defined, including prime $\mathcal{F}$-ideal and $\mathcal{S}$-ideal forms. Additionally, we are examining the interplay between these concepts and other forms of prime ideals, such as strongly prime and mixed prime ideals, in the context of rings with specific properties, including reduced rings and integral domains. Specifically, we are looking at the relationship between different types of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals and establishing connections between these various forms.

We present new findings for two semileptonic decay processes, $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a lepton-neutrino pair, and $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ with the same pair, utilizing data from 3.8 inverse femtobarns of LHCb collected data at 8 TeV center-of-mass energy. By analyzing the decay of $\rho$ into a pair of charged pions, our calculations yield total branching fractions of $5.10\,\% \times 10^{-4}$ and $2.74\,\% \times 10^{-4}$ respectively, with the uncertainty primarily stemming from the measurement of $B$ hadron quantities.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional spectroscopy technique, enabling more efficient thulium-doped water absorption spectroscopy. By utilizing an integrated photonic device with features like high quality factor and small mode volume, it interacted with photons for extended periods, facilitating interaction with individual photons multiple times. In comparison to other broadly-tuned tunable laser sources, this approach offers the benefits of low power, compactness, and affordability. We've successfully demonstrated an alternative approach to spectroscopy by combining a photonic device with lasing in the normal dispersion region, then scanning the frequency in an absorption spectrum. This innovation could facilitate the development of low-power and chip-scale systems for remote sensing. Our work also provides the foundation for developing highly sensitive photonic systems and complex systems with multiple channels for future photonic applications.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

Several local authorities face difficulties in efficiently and effectively managing automated road damage assessment. While several features are vital for an ideal solution, set against a limited budget and available resources, finding a fully functional system is impossible. As road damage evaluation systems require substantial storage for raw image data and processed images, as well as a powerful server for pre-processing, setting up such a system can be challenging, especially when these resources are not locally available. To overcome these obstacles, this study presents a novel solution comprising three key components: (a) a microservices-based architecture using Docker and Kubernetes to streamline server configuration, (b) a serverless FUSE-based filesystem using AWS Lambda to simplify local data storage, and (c a networkless container registry using AWS S3 to store shared data across multiple servers. The proposed microservices architecture, serverless filesystem, and networkless container registry address the need for easy local data management, as well as a reliable and low-maintenance framework for automated road damage assessment systems.

Imitation learning has become a preferred method for agent training due to its ability to leverage expert demonstrations, in contrast to the challenging task of defining reward functions required in reinforcement learning. However, imitation learning often lacks explicit guidance on the underlying task, making the policy vulnerable to defective behaviors such as noise and redundant actions. This can result in suboptimal performance, particularly in complex environments. This paper introduces a novel imitation learning framework called implicit world model guided imitation learning (iwmg), which enhances imitation learning by integrating an implicit environment model trained during the process. Specifically, iwgmodel predicts future expert actions based on current state transitions, allowing the agent policy to capitalize on these predictions. This approach reduces dependence on expert noises and unnecessary actions, thereby improving the agent's performance. Furthermore, iwgmodel exhibits reduced generalization limitations and superior environment adaptability. Experimental results validate the proposed iwgmodel's superior performance and its ability to generalize and adapt to various environments.

Previous studies indicate that the initial universe was not conducive to forming life-supporting elements and molecules necessary for habitation,, due to the lack of water and carbon-based compounds, and, the tendency toward forming heavier elements. We hypothesize, however, that the process can be ongoing in the early universe, and that secondary star and galaxy formation was possible, given that the law of conservation applies universally. We examine the role of magnetic field amplification in the early universe, particularly its impact on the formation of protostars and planets within protostellar systems. We suggest that the gravitational collapse of dense gas clouds, resulting in the spiraling in of smaller clouds, could lead to the formation of multiple protostellar systems. Ultimately, the end-products of such processes could include water, minerals, and other essential elements, potentially laying the groundwork for the formation of life.

Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves finding relationships between itemsets within a given database. The frequency of items in the dataset determines the analysis, with higher-frequency items having greater significance. We propose a novel method called Fuzzy High Frequency Items Association Rule Mining to detect relationship-based patterns even when dataset items have varying frequencies. Another innovation involves refining how we calculate the confidence and support metrics.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 2009 and 2019, involving offenders sentenced to probation with or without mental health treatment, demonstrates that mental health treatment recipients are less likely to return to the justice system.  These findings highlight the value of mental health treatment in the justice system.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Radio maps are being explored as a means to provide reliable spatial location information and precise situational awareness for wireless communications, including the next generation of unmanned aerial vehicles. Current techniques utilizing geo定位 have shown limitations due to their dependence on detailed, real-time environmental knowledge and specialized equipment. Leveraging the capabilities of deep learning and the spatial and temporal data in radio map construction, spatially accurate positions can be automatically extracted and adapted to varying environmental conditions. This paper introduces a novel radio map construction method based on a machine learning model that incorporates both spatial and time-related visual information.

This paper outlines a novel approach in computational systems to identify unusual patterns in discrete time series data and space-time images. We present an algorithm that incorporates Hidden Markov Models into a two-stage process. The first stage involves using a single Hidden Markov Model to detect potential hidden states from the observed data. The second stage utilizes a spatial grid to cluster these states and establish a normal distribution. We then apply a series of modifications to the algorithm to improve its performance, including making it adaptive to the observed data, removing spatial dependencies to prevent state collapse and introducing a stochastic refinement step to remove unwanted stuck states. The method demonstrates its effectiveness on synthetic data sets and a real-world example of sound space-time analysis, showing unusual patterns in a dataset of sounds generated by a group of animals.

This research delves into person verification through unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal approaches, focusing on using eye movement data in addition to face and hand biometrics. A substantial and diverse dataset of 7,539 eye movement videos from the appearance of a single face to interaction with two books was collected, along with 2,500 images and 15,000 face and hand biometric samples, within a controlled laboratory setting. The results show a notable increase in accuracy when using a trimodal verification system in comparison to unimodal and bimodal systems. Notably, a significant improvement of 40% in Equal Error Rate was achieved with a trimodal system over state-of-the-art face and eye movement verification methods.

Recent breakthroughs in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) have been largely attributed to AsrNet, including the use of Transformer and Conformer models. These models were able to improve their accuracy when trained with diverse data augmentation techniques. Building on this success, our research investigates the effect of ASR's continued training with augmented data similar to that used in Amazon Alexa. To achieve this, we incorporated noise simulation, speech manipulation, and speech transformation techniques into our continuous ASR training process. Notably, our findings show that even though individual augmentation methods do not yield optimal results, combining them all enables ASR models to maintain high recognition accuracy in real-world settings.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, with a known function $f(\cdot|\cdot)$. When a random variable $Y$ follows a distribution that is a mixture of $f(\cdot|\theta)$ with a probability measure $\pi(\cdot)$ on $\Omega$, and observations of $Y$ are available, the task is to estimate the mixing distribution $\pi(\cdot)$. A method known as Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimation (GMLE) was initially proposed in 1988 by Geman and Macdonald, and in this note, recent findings on the nonparametric GMLE are summarized, covering the basic theory, performance in specific scenarios, and more recent developments.

Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is a pressing issue in various data analysis contexts. To address this gap, we introduce One-Sided Differential Privacy, a novel framework that takes into account the differing knowledge levels between data recorders and potential intruders. Understanding that data recorders possess comprehensive data access, while intruders only have limited knowledge of the data, we explore scenarios where recorders aim to share information securely. One-Sided Differential Privacy guarantees accurate analysis results in the absence of an intruder, while ensuring privacy when a intruder is present. We derive an closed-form expression for an optimal mechanism under specific loss functions, including squared loss and Laplace loss. We also provide closed-form solutions for specific use cases, including when knowledge differences are binary or when the intruder has a bounded number of known data points. We further extend the approach to handle multiple intruders and discuss its relationship with existing research on adversarial DP. We also analyze recorders' risk levels based on varying numbers of intrudues. We extend OSDP to scenarios with multiple recorders, thus giving rise to the concept of Two-Sided Differential Privacy, where intrudues have access to data from one of the recorders. We provide closed-form expressions for optimal OSDP mechanisms under specific loss functions.

In protoplanetary disks, it is not uncommon to observe substructures in the gas that coincide with excess emissions from small particles, which are potential indicators of emerging planetary systems. To gain a deeper understanding of how gas and solid particles interact in protoplanetary disks around main-sequence stars and developing planetary systems, a detailed examination of these structures has been conducted using ALMA and VLT/SINFONI data. This study employs a dynamical model that simulates the dynamics of three disks containing developing planetary systems characterized by various types of gas substructures generated by one or more planetary traps. By using high-resolution ALMA images in molecular carbon monoxide to map the gas dynamics, effective temperatures, stellar irradiation effects, and gas pressure locations, disk models are inferred. Concurrently, radiation and particle hydrodynamics are simulated to assess their influence on the observed structures. Measurements of total dust masses in the gas substructures are made using dust scattering, which reveals that these complex gas features can arise from the interactions of multiple bodies such as planetary systems, blocks of particles, or regions with decreased transport efficiency. Accordingly, disk substructures cannot serve as a definitive marker of planetary accretion on main-sequence stars without further investigation. This study lays the groundwork for future detailed investigations utilizing high-resolution ALMA images in molecular carbon monoxide, which will provide insights into the gas dynamics of disks.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational performance and efficiency.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint that state process follow a predetermined trajectory. The analysis is carried out under minimal regularity assumptions on the involved functions.

Recent analyses of the Milky Way have revealed complex, string-like formations of stars, often referred to as stellar strings, within the galaxy's bulge and outer regions. Researchers stand in awe of these intriguing structures, yet their significance, whether they hold aesthetic value or scientific importance, remains a subject of debate. A study by Bostwick et al. (2023) investigated a stellar string located in the Milky Way's outer region and discovered that it appears to be a collection of dispersing star clusters along its length. The study suggests that the clusters within the string formed around one billion years ago through cloud fragmentation, resulting in the string's leftward expansion at a speed of approximately 300 km/second. According to the study, the string will likely dissolve into a smooth, symmetrical galactic distribution within the next 50 million years, effectively resolving the controversy surrounding stellar strings as either real objects or mere visual illusions.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies primarily investigate color coordination, yet style and other aspects of outfit harmony are equally important and have been largely overlooked. Our approach to style alignment involves extracting feature representations using a deep neural network and applying a approach to visualize and reduce dimensions specifically for style comparison. Moreover, our style-aligned method is applicable to various style extraction features, including visual and textual, and we demonstrate this by incorporating Cloze-pair data from the Fashion Neural Style Transfer project.

Quantum resource theory categorizes quantum states into specific non-resourceful states and quantum resources, enabling the study of fundamental properties and conversion rules between them. Focusing on phases within quantum systems, we investigate the phase resource theory structure. We demonstrate that any quantum state can be classified as either a quantum resource or a non-resourceful state among non-entangled states, with the latter comprising the tensor product of phases, pure mixtures of local basis states, and basis states. We then examine how phase resources can be transformed into non-resourceful phases, either using measurements or without measurements, finding that added resources are necessary when measurements are prohibited, with multiple instances even exhibiting non-asymptotic consumption.

As the number of devices using cross-device federated learning grows, managing a large-scale distributed model update efficiently becomes a significant challenge. Current solutions, often reliant on a centralized server, struggle to scale due to communication constraints between the server and each individual device. The communication system within a group of participating devices, however, can effectively support inter-group model data exchange. This paper explores applying inter-group communication to scale up cross-device federated learning, specifically introducing a novel solution that leverages inter-group communication and eliminates reliance on a central server. A new, scalable CDFL framework, called GCDFL, is proposed, which effectively handles both exchange between full model updates and gradient updates. The scalability and performance benefits of GCDFL are demonstrated through extensive experimental results.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant semigroups. As a concrete application, we implement a unified approach to the functional calculus for a family of operators including the derivative, Laplacian, and fractional Laplacian operators.

Recent research has explored Hawking radiation in a four-dimensional universe originating from black holes in four-dimensional space. The radiation rates were computed using the path integral approach, taking into account the influence of a finite four-dimensional dimension. The study demonstrated that in the presence of a separate 4D dimension, Hawking radiation is emitted more rapidly. The total mass of the black hole was calculated by considering the interference of partial waves, and the resulting analysis showed a logarithmic increase in the final black hole mass. The investigation into this mass also included the effect of the black hole's charge.

A floating raft made of particles offers a model system that allows researchers to study self-assembly processes in an environment undergoing expansion. When external forces cause the underlying liquid's surface to increase in area, the raft experiences thermal fluctuations and eventually collapses due to these changes. By experimenting with the raft's failure patterns under various liquid expansion rates and influencing factors, such as temperature, we discovered how the size of the raft grows over time and how its size is affected by these variables. Additionally, the data we gathered can be theoretically explained using the laws governing the laws governing the dynamics of a critical sandpile.

We utilized a comprehensive full-band model to investigate the effects of lattice matching and uniaxial strain on gallium nitride, in relation to the crystal structures of various nitride materials, as well as its Fermi level in uncompressed states. The findings demonstrate that lattice matching with group-III materials causes the heavy and light hole bands to invert in GaN, leading to a mixed character in these bands. The implementation of compressive strain eliminates this hole band inversion. Additionally, we observed that compressive strain results in the splitting of valence band degeneracy and alters the position of the Fermi level under compressive strain. The calculated spin-orbit energy values show that it increases with the application of compressive strain. The calculations also indicate that it lattice matching with group-II materials causes the spin-orbit energy to rise significantly and shift the Fermi level into the valence band, leading to a considerable broadening of valence bands under compressive strain. The results also show that it lattice matching with group-IV materials causes the spin-orbit energy to decrease and the Fermi level to be positioned within a hole-like state, leading to the broadening of valence bands under compressive strain. The calculations also reveal that it lattice matching with group-II materials leads to the inversion of both the valence and conduction bands, due to N donor states and the transfer of holes and electrons from the host material to the GaN layer. Our novel TD learning approach incorporates Gaussian Process regression into the Generalized Eligibility Trace framework to enable robots to efficiently navigate dynamic marine environments. By combining Gaussian Process regression's ability to model temporal dynamics and outgoing state trajectories with TD learning's ability to learn valuable state representations, our method enhances the efficiency of policy learning and allows robots to generate informative trajectories without the need for extensive explorations. The experimental results using simulated and real marine robots demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in learning valuable state representations and achieving efficient policy learning.

We isothermally parameterize surfaces and classify them based the holomorphicity of their Hopf differential. For surfaces with a mean curvature line geometry, we extend this classification. The geometry of isothermic surfaces can be expressed as a chain of linear transformations. We demonstrate that their equivalence, up to congruence, is determined by a normal form, which we use to classify locally their locally their congruence classes.

We analyze the $L^2$-operator $\mathcal{E}_n(f \mapsto Cf)$, which approximates $f(x)$ with $Cf(x) = \mathbb{E}(f(X_n)|X_{k_n}=x)$, in a Hilbert space setting under certain constraints. We demonstrate that for a suitable choice of $\{k_n\}$, $\mathcal{E}_n$ can be represented as a sum of Hilbert-Schmidt operators with uniformly bounded norms. We also compute the approximation error $\| \mathcal{E}_n - \mathrm{Id} \|_{\mathrm{Sch}}$ and show its convergence rate is the same as $\| \mathrm{Id} - \mathcal{E}_n \|$. This result is then applied in various Hilbert space-valued nonparametric series models, including the Hilbert space-valued random walk and a Hilbert space-valary short-memory model, to obtain $\sqrt{T}$-consistent and sqrt{T}-consistent and asymptotically normal limits for $\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{LS}}$.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind. We explore and define the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and their associated properties. We derive recurrence relations, identities and present comparable results for $\lambda$-analogues of Whitney-type $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. We also introduce $\lambda$-analogues of Dowling polynomials and provide a formula reminiscent of the Dobinski-like formula.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance to improve performance of subsequent applications. Despite its potential, the majority of existing research ignores temporal dimensions. In contrast, a small number of studies focus on encoding temporal patterns within dynamic knowledge graphs but neglect the temporal scopes of individual facts. As a result, the informational value contained within temporal scopes remains underutilized in current time-aware knowledge graph embedding models. To bridge this gap, a novel embedding method called TemKGE is proposed. TemKGE takes into account the temporal ranges of entities and facts when training models, without requiring any additional data. This novel approach yields notable enhancements in both time-independent and time-sensitive evaluation metrics when compared to existing time-aware KGE methods.

This research confirms Conjecture 1.4 proposed in Matui and Tomatsu's work on Strong Shift Equivalence and Graph C*-algebras. It also provides a detailed comparison between two concepts: (a) strong shift equivalence among graph C*-algebras, and (b) Morita equivalence of their underlying graph algebras. This comparison serves as the foundation to prove that (a) implies (b). Furthermore, if the graph is finite but not necessarily of uniform row length, we show that (b) is equivalent to a broader concept, called Morita equivalence up to covering (c). We establish the relationships a implies c implies b, and identify the conditions under which b implies a, thus fully answering Conjecture 3.6 in Matui and Tomatsu's "Strong Shift Equivalence and Graph C*-algebras".

In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions.

To effectively answer questions for large-scale, encyclopedic Q&A systems, Language Models need access to external knowledge. Current research in this area often trains specialized models, but our study demonstrates the effectiveness of using pre-trained models in combination with knowledge graphs for this purpose. We develop and release several GQA variants based on the Flan-T5 foundation model, leveraging the Wikidata knowledge graph, as well as Flan-QA, as starting points. Our results reveal that fine-tuning these pre-trained models on the Wikidata entity-grounding dataset yields high-quality GQA systems that surpass the performance of the original Flan-T5 model on the FLASK benchmark, highlighting a more promising direction for the development of language models.

We have developed a novel method to create high dimensional expanders by 
expanding upon a well-known concept called basic expander graphs. In our paper, 
we propose a novel framework for high dimensional expanders and use the new 
framework to efficiently generate random high dimensional expanders. To the 
best of our knowledge, this is the sole known constructive approach to generating
random high dimensional expanders. Furthermore, a specific special case of our
framework yields a simple, explicit construction of random high dimensional
expanders that likely possesses some statistically ideal properties.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. To mitigate this, we propose a novel approach that optimizes prompts by refining them using feedback in the form of choice-based answers. Our experimental results demonstrate that this strategy consistently enhances language model performance, particularly when the approach tailors prompts to specific tasks. Moreover, incorporating choice-based answers in the prompt not only improves performance but also contributes positively.

We have computed the Benois $\mathcal{L}$-invariants for weight one cuspforms and their corresponding adjoint representations. Furthermore, our calculations extend Gross' $p$-adic regulator to non-critical values of cuspforms with prime conductors. These results come with a Sato-Tate distribution estimate supported by numerical experiments.

We introduce a innovative method to detect complex multifrequency microwave electric fields with high precision using Rydberg atoms, which can be done simultaneously and independently. This approach allows for the simultaneous measurement of multiple frequencies, which is not possible with traditional atom-based methods limited to single-frequency detection, nor with existing RADIOLINO systems that require extensive time for atom-based multitone measurements. Additionally, our method offers sub-fossil Hz frequency resolution and parts-per-billion frequency accuracy, making it a highly accurate tool. Furthermore, it provides an alternative method to detect multiple multitone frequencies at once, which can be applied to characterize atom clocks and improve their accuracy.

UGC 8839, a low surface brightness spiral galaxy, is characterized by substantial off-axis star formation. The phenomenon is primarily attributed to its unusually large and distinct bar, as well as an extremely low gas pressure in its disk. Due to this instability, the formation of stars is shifted far from the galaxy's center, as observed in H-alpha images, which reveal an offset of about 12 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's potential minimum. Although an analytical ring potential is inconsistent with these observations, a bar potential derived from the observations closely reveals the predicted minimum to precisely match its position and size. Due to its low central star density, this phenomenon is only visible in low surface brightness galaxies, which harbor large, stable bars and substantial amounts of off-axis star formation.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range of 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under a specific growth constraint.

Using the Mars Atmosphere and Volumes–Investigation Mission's neutral mass spectrometer, researchers have identified daily and diurnal gravity waves in the mesosphere and mesosphere of Mars. Their findings are similar to those of Earth's gravity waves, although the sources differ. A particular interest lies in the connection between the gravity waves and the daily and seasonal gravity wave forecasts made using the Mars Global Climate Model. A preliminary correlation analysis has been carried out to investigate this connection. A statistical measure, known as Pearson's correlation coefficient, was employed. A significant correlation was found between the gravity wave intensity and the daily wind speed at 3700 K, with coefficients of 0.39 and 0.32 for the summer and spring seasons respectively. A stronger correlation of 0.5 was found between the gravity wave intensity and the GCM-predicted daily wind speed. A significant correlation of 0.42 was found between the gravity wave intensity and the GCM-predicted seasonal wind speed. However, these results do not necessarily imply a causal link. These findings are consistent with the possibility that the daily and seasonal forecasts capture a significant portion of the gravity wave activity. Additionally, the correlation between the gravity wave intensity and the GCM-predicted daily wind speed appears seasonal in nature, exhibiting the strongest correlation in the summer and the weakest in the spring. These findings are consistent with the possibility that the daily and seasonal forecasts capture a significant portion of the gravity wave

The LHC is set to initiate data collection in 2009, including information gathered not only from conventional proton-proton and heavy ion collisions but also from the novel Ultra Peripheral Collisions of lead ions. These occur when the long, tightly packed proton, consisting of numerous pseudo-two-dimensional structures, reveals its individual, space-like separated valence quarks. These can behave like independent quarks, leading to new types of collisions such as $p + p \rightarrow p + p + \gamma + \gamma$ and $ Pb + Pb \rightarrow Pb + Pb + \gamma + \gamma$. Additionally, the interaction of the long, space-like separated quarks makes lead-lead collisions not only heavy ion collisions but also photon and hadron exchanges. Researchers anticipate that the data from these ULPP collisions will offer unique insights, enabling the creation of new observables and analysis methods that were previously only possible with photon collisions.

Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through deep learning hold great promise.
A breakthrough model demonstrated the potential to create high-fidelity, short-duration audio clips at a relatively rapid pace. 
Building upon this, we aim to enhance its application in sound effect creation by improving its two main limitations. 
First, the current model struggles to produce distinct instruments, likely due to its reliance on text-based prompts. 
To address this, we employ a new instrument classifier that enables prompt augmentation with specific instrument choices, thus allowing for more targeted audio generation. 
Second, the audio clips produced by the model are limited to under 10 seconds. 
To overcome this, we utilize an audio segmenter to divide any given event into smaller timeframes and then recombine the generated audio clips, enabling the synthesis of effects lasting up to several minutes. 
We evaluate our approach using a combination of automatic and manual evaluation methods. 
While the automated system highlights areas for improvement, particularly in acoustic quality, we find that our model produces synched, clear instruments with zero overlap and distinct onsets. 
Overall, the audio generated meets the requirements of most effect libraries, with a maximum duration of 2 minutes, 20 seconds. 
Notably, the model excels in music and complex sounds but falls short in voice generation.

Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural language, time series and visual data, enabling a wide range of tasks such as translation, classification, image recognition and more. To facilitate the ease of implementation and comparison of various recurrent network architectures, we introduce an intuitive and straightforward Python package, RNNLayer, which unifies the code for different recurrent network layers, including but not limited to LSTMs, GRUs and 1-1D-CNNs.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, and attributes this finding to the broader concept of 'economic irreversibility,' illustrating its analogy to the principles of thermodynamics. A fundamental inequality provides a framework for the implementation of such measures. A case study demonstrates the practical application of this model in the context of Italy, and uses it to interpret the moderate measures introduced during the second lockdown.

The development of base models and their training datasets is a time-consuming process, prompting the idea of accelerating training through the utilization of pre-trained 'expert' shards. A critical challenge arises in apportioning credit for the final model's performance among these shards, leading to the computation of Shapley values as a transparent and equitable solution. Due to the infeasibility of exact calculations, we introduce a simplified approximation called Credit for Learning on Subsets (CLoS), which is based on learning curve approximations using quadratic functions. The efficacy of our method was evaluated on image classification and sequence-to-sequence translation datasets, demonstrating that our method not only provides a satisfactory approximation in most cases but also identifies key shard characteristics influencing final model quality.

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices.

This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant structural transformation, altering its symmetry and modifying the positions of its Sn atoms. The application of pressure has been found to consistently diminish the anomalous Hall effect, a phenomenon attributed to the compression's impact on the material's band structure and its stabilization of a particular magnetic state. The results offer a comprehensive understanding of how external pressure can stabilize antiferromagnetic stability and adjust magnetic properties in Mn$_3$Sn.

Formal knowledge acquisition through Natural Language Processing (NLP) is heavily reliant on the success of relation extraction (RE), a crucial task that赋grants a particular logical structure to gathered information from textual data. However, the current data sparsity poses a significant challenge, hindering conventional RE methods. To tackle this issue, we propose RELAX, a novel approach that enriches data by producing implicit relations, which are then integrated into a pre-trained language model to facilitate knowledge representation. RELAX operates through two main components, an inductive reasoning module that predicts latent relations and a reinforcement learning module that optimizes the former through a data-driven graph. RELAX is empirically shown to significantly outperform state-of-the-art RE models in RE tasks under data-sparse settings, with open-source implementation and accompanying data available at this link: https://github.com/axiayaxiayaxiayaxia/RE-LAX.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set, a smaller compact set with multiple components, and a intermediate region. Our main focus lies in analyzing the properties of its eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, with an emphasis on the influence of the intermediate region's shape on these properties. Moreover, we derive precise asymptotic estimates for the first eigenvalue in this problem.

We investigate the significant challenges in modeling complex systems represented as graphs, and how these systems, composed of multiple interconnected entities, can be more effectively modeled using hypergraphs, which allow for the representation of interactions between multiple systems simultaneously. To capture both the structural and temporal aspects of these dynamic systems, we develop a method for generating temporally varying hypergraphs, enabling us to observe how these systems evolve over time. This approach is demonstrated on real-world time-series data and brings a new perspective to both visualizing and analyzing the changing characteristics of temporally varying systems.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document their findings and analysis. This information is highly valuable in the field, guiding researchers and researchers in analyzing medical conditions. Deep learning techniques have made significant advancements in medical field, specifically in processing medical images without anatomical references. Images without proper anatomical context can be hard to interpret, so it's essential to incorporate anatomical information. Several works, such as Unet, ResNet, and Dilated Conv, have shown potential, but they involve either a high computational cost or produce inaccurate results. Our proposed AN-Rasnet model utilizes the PR-AN image with anatomical information and removes unnecessary data using the Attention Gate module. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of the AN-Rasnet model by achieving superior performance compared to existing techniques.

Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a limited range. Subsequent work by a different researcher shown that the range is at least half as large. Thurstons example also served as the only known case where the upper boundary of the range was achieved. Building on this, a new study discovers an infinite collection of hyperbolic 3-manifolds with Euler classes of taut foliations that are limited to a range just below the upper boundary. These new findings are complemented by a new demonstration that, in certain types of hyperbolic 3-manifolds, the Euler classes of tight contact structures have a limited range that is comparable to that of taut foliations. This research validates a hypothesis initially proposed by Thurston. Moreover, a new study finds that, in certain types of hyperbolic 3-manifolds, the set of Euler classes of tight contact structures is not as limited as the set of Euler classes of tight contact structures in related tight manifolds.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy in spherical harmonic components and mutual information between dipoles better accommodate intricate structures, yet these concepts remain theoretical and may not be directly relevant to emission directionality.

Our analysis of 3,500 global cryptocurrencies reveals four distinct classes based on their investment characteristics. To classify these digital assets, we applied a clustering method to multiple factors, including price stability, return patterns, and on-chain usage. The first category consists of stablecoins, representing a small portion of the market at $115 billion. These coins exhibit stability comparable to major financial assets due to tethering mechanisms. The second category, comprising 22 cryptocurrencies including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and BNB, serves as a store of value. These coins exhibit high volatility but a unique non-negative skew in returns, reminiscent of gold. Bitcoin's and Ether's low transaction costs and high smart contract capabilities make them the foundation of the decentralized finance (DeFi) ecosystem. They also serve as a bridge between on-chain and off-chain markets. The remaining cryptocurrencies are divided into value-trading and utility-based categories, reflecting their primary market focus.

By integrating analytical methods including field theory, probability and integrability, we resolve the large deviation issue of the KPZ equation at early time periods. Expanding the existing weak noise theory, which reformulates large deviations into a nonlinear hydrodynamics problem, we reveal its complete solvability through a link with the integrability of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Employing the inverse scattering technique and a newly developed Fredholm determinant framework, we solve the problem with the aid of the Whittaker function and thereby derive an explicit expression for the rate function.

The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is a subject of debate, with observations from Cluster and MMS missions revealing specific features. To address this debate, various mechanisms are examined through kinetic simulations, which reproduce the observed clustering of critical wave modes in the plasma. This clustering arises from nonlinear interactions among various wave modes and is characterized by distinct morphologies at different scales. Two mechanisms emerge as primary contributors: the ability of electrostatic modes to efficiently absorb energy and transfer it to electron heating, and the efficient phase mixing of large-scale compressive parallel propagating modes in small-scale perpendicular directions. These findings are consistent with previous predictions and suggest that plasma turbulence is composed of interacting and mixing wave modes with unique characteristics.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the LCLS demonstrate successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2.82 nm bandwidth at the pulse's end, matching its mean intensity during amplification.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order term arises in the model. Along with a bottom friction model and a Boussinesq approximation that accounts for fluid density variations due to temperature changes, the model leads to a system of five ordinary differential equations governing temperature and velocity profiles. Unlike traditional models, this framework enables analytical solutions of both temperature and velocity distributions. These solutions are validated through numerical simulations of a daily cycle, including simulations of mixed convection, pure convection, and transitional convection.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster Simulated Annealing variant produced a notable evaluation of the state's
2020 districting plan.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor called GHOG, which effectively captures defects by distinguishing between fabric and defects based on their visual characteristics. Following a region-based detection method, a novel approach called defect-aware fusion is employed to reconstruct defective fabric regions, preserving pattern continuity. This approach outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in detecting defects on patterned fabric images.

Target-driven visual navigation using deep reinforcement learning (DL) has made significant progress, but current methods often struggle with sample efficiency and stability issues. To address these limitations, we propose integrating feedback provided by a semantic semantic salience (SSM) metric. This feedback guides the DL-based decision-making process, allowing the policy network to converge more quickly. The SSM metric, calculated at each step, provides a backward sample efficiency and stability. This feedback is delivered as a combined reward and priority memory update value, derived from the semantic structures in the current and prior observations. The backward sample efficiency and stability introduced by the SSM metric is demonstrated through extensive experiments conducted in the AI2-Minigov environment. Our approach also shows improved results, validated by the sample efficiency, stability, and final performance of the existing A3C method.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at the origin and reaches infinity, we determine the maximum allowable rate of change of Bondi mass in the Einstein theory. This maximum rate is directly proportional to Dyson's maximum luminosity and is not influenced by any specific constant, including the speed of light. We then explore how this limit is affected in scalar-tensor gravity theories, where it can be exceeded under certain conditions, such as when the coupling between the scalar field and the Einstein scalar are relatively small.

We've developed a sophisticated framework for simulating the development of population III binary remnants within dense population II/XXI nuclei. This framework incorporates the spatial distribution and merger timing of such remnants based on a power-law initial mass function. Our model assumes a power-law distribution for initial masses ranging from $5 M_{\odot}$ to $100 M_{\odot}$. This enables us to calculate the merging rate of such population III binary remnants in such nuclei and analyze the gravitational wave background generated by these mergers. Our model accounts for various power-law exponents ($\beta$) and is further enhanced with a specific mass function that features a peak at $30 M_{\odot}$. Our findings indicate that approximately 10-25% of population III binary remnants will merge within such nuclei, with merger times ranging from 1000 to 10000000 years. Our simulation also predicts a significant accumulation of population III binary remnants near the center of such nuclei, ultimately resulting in a notable background of gravitational waves in nearby galaxies.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on active and reactive power control strategies for ESS.

The meson loops theory proposes that the radiative decay of X(3872) to J/psi pi gamma is governed by meson loops, with the radiative part factorized and the decay dominantly proceeding through X(3872) to pi D*bar K and back to J/psi pi with photon emission from virtual mesons. This framework successfully explains the large value of branching ratio, preferential decay to charged modes, and kinematic mass dependence. By applying this model, predictions are made for several unobserved X(3872) decays and their potential observation.

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
However, previous attempts to develop text-based game agents using reinforcement learning have relied on using sound effects and background music as part of the reward system, effectively using sensory information to guide their decisions.
This strategy led to the emergence of "cheating" behaviors, where the model used sound effects to make informed decisions.
In contrast, our study aims to create more authentic agents that learn solely from textual information.
We present a novel strategy to create high-performing text-only agents with improved consistency and consistency in social interactions with other in-game characters.
Our research involves creating data-driven virtual agents for the adventure game Mystery House.
We compare the effectiveness of these agents to sound-augmented agents, finding that the sound-based agents rely on audio cues rather than text, leading to inconsistent decision-making and interaction patterns.
Specifically, the audio-assisted agents rely on sound effects, leading to erratic behavior and flawed decision-making, while the consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency, consistency,

The interaction between magnetic fields and defects in materials is a complex problem with implications for both conventional and topological insulators. In Topological Insulators, the behavior of electrons is characterized by the transport of spin along the edges, which can be disrupted by the presence of defects. The research focuses on the effect of a specific defect type, known as an edge dislocation with a shear strain, and its impact on spin and charge transport. By considering the strain-induced changes to the material's band structure, it is found that a quasi-edge state forms and the spin and charge are quantized along certain paths. Furthermore, the characteristics of this quantization are influenced by two key factors, the spin orientation and a universal scaling parameter.
